tldr: Targeting manipulation tasks with moving objects where fast reactions are critical, this paper proposes "ReflexBench," an evaluation benchmark that accurately simulates inference latency, and "ReflexVLA," a lightweight VLA that incorporates latent future prediction and speedups via CUDA Graph. Despite being a compact 1B model, it cuts inference latency roughly in half and significantly outperforms 7B-scale models on dynamic manipulation tasks.
hero_caption: Overview of the research. Left: Key challenges faced by existing VLAs (motion unawareness, lack of future prediction, and large inference latency). Top right: The three core pillars of the proposed ReflexVLA to address them. Bottom: Six dynamic tasks in the ReflexBench evaluation benchmark, which faithfully reproduces inference latency.
overview:
In recent robotics research, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that integrate vision, language, and action into a single foundation model have attracted considerable attention. However, most existing benchmarks only consider static manipulation tasks, freezing the simulator clock during model inference. This prevents properly evaluating dynamic tasks where inference latency is fatal in the real world, such as picking objects off a conveyor belt or catching a rolling ball.

To address this gap, the authors developed "ReflexBench," a benchmark for dynamic manipulation that decouples simulator stepping from robot control, allowing inference latency to be flexibly configured and reproduced. Furthermore, to conquer this demanding dynamic environment, they propose "ReflexVLA," an efficient VLA model. ReflexVLA skillfully combines three approaches: (1) training with latent future prediction in the feature space of a frozen vision foundation model, (2) multi-frame temporal fusion within intermediate layers of the vision backbone without increasing the token count fed to the language model, and (3) deployment latency reductions via batched visual encoding and CUDA Graph replay.

Experiments show that despite its compact 1B parameter footprint, ReflexVLA cuts inference latency from 125.1 ms to 65.0 ms (nearly in half) and achieves an average success rate of 50.4% on ReflexBench. This significantly outperforms larger models such as the 7B OpenVLA-OFT and 4B $\pi_{0.5}$. Furthermore, it maintains competitive state-of-the-art accuracy of 97.2% on the standard static benchmark LIBERO, and real-world robot arm experiments demonstrate its ability to reliably capture fast-moving targets.
contributions: Constructed ReflexBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark containing six reaction-critical tasks that faithfully reflects inference latency and the effects of synchronous and asynchronous control.

Introduced an auxiliary task predicting future states in the latent feature space of frozen DINOv3 rather than raw image pixels, enabling dynamic representation learning with minimal computational cost.
Developed an efficient temporal modeling approach that fuses local multi-frame features at intermediate layers of the vision backbone without increasing the token count fed to the language model.

Halved inference latency via batched visual encoding and CUDA Graph replay, demonstrating that a 1B model can outperform much larger VLAs on dynamic tasks in both simulation and real-world experiments.

sections.heading: From a Static to a Moving World: Why Current VLAs Struggle with Dynamic Tasks
sections.summary: While conventional VLA models show high generalization on static tasks, they face major challenges in dynamic environments due to inference latency and lack of future prediction. Aiming to reconcile future prediction with fast inference, this paper presents the ReflexBench benchmark and the predictive, fast ReflexVLA model.
sections.details:
With the rise of large-scale vision-language models, VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models that learn robot control policies directly from multimodal data have stepped into the spotlight. Their ability to follow natural language instructions and generalize to unseen tasks and environments has progressed remarkably.

However, current VLAs have a major blind spot: they struggle severely with operations in dynamic environments that demand fast reactions and future prediction. Most existing methods generate actions conditioned only on a single current image frame. Because of inference latency, a temporal mismatch arises between the perceived state of the world and actual robot actuation. In tasks like intercepting a moving object or catching a rolling ball, this tiny delay leads directly to failure.

Prior work has explored dynamic manipulation benchmarks, future prediction models, or model compression for acceleration in isolation. However, attempting to predict the future usually increases compute and worsens latency, whereas pursuing speed alone prevents future-oriented decision-making. Research combining both has been insufficient. This paper tackles this unexplored challenge by building ReflexBench to faithfully simulate real-world latency, and designing ReflexVLA to achieve both fast inference and future prediction.

sections.heading: Where Dynamic Benchmarks Meet Fast Execution
sections.summary: The authors review two lines of related work: dynamic manipulation benchmarks and efficient VLA models. This work sets itself apart by explicitly modeling inference latency while integrating future prediction and system optimizations.
sections.details:
Related work falls broadly into two streams.

The first is benchmarks for dynamic manipulation. Recent studies focusing on object motion, perception/execution delays, and spatiotemporal reasoning have highlighted how vulnerable existing VLAs are to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks did not faithfully model inference latency across synchronous and asynchronous execution regimes. ReflexBench decouples simulator stepping from control, enabling much more realistic latency evaluations.

The second is the design of efficient VLA models. Active efforts include reducing model size (such as SmolVLA and VLA-Adapter) and tailoring architectures or inference systems for real-time control (such as FASTER and VLASH). Nevertheless, these works focus primarily on pruning compute or raising execution frequencies. They have not deeply investigated the core question of how inference latency and future prediction capability interact in dynamic tasks. This research aims to address both at the same time.

sections.heading: Facing Latency Head-on: A Dynamic Benchmark Simulating Real-World Delays
sections.summary: To accurately evaluate control latency in the real world, the authors built ReflexBench, a benchmark featuring six dynamic tasks and a blocking mechanism that strictly reproduces synchronous and asynchronous inference latency in simulation.
sections.details:
Most conventional robot simulation environments pause the simulator clock while the policy model performs inference. Under this setup, whether inference takes 100 ms or 1 second makes no difference, making it impossible to evaluate the deployment mismatch on physical hardware. ReflexBench fundamentally resolves this issue.

### Task Suite
ReflexBench provides six representative tasks where fast reactions are essential:
- Conveyor Belt Pick-and-Place
- Ball Catching
- Whack-a-Mole
- Rolling Ball Interception
- Ball Throwing
- Rotating Peg Insertion

### Data Collection Pipeline
Collecting high-quality demonstration trajectories with moving objects is difficult using human teleoperation or simple hardcoded scripts. The authors therefore built a planning-based pipeline that decomposes tasks into subgoals and plans motions by forecasting future object trajectories from positions and velocities. For select tasks with complex physical interactions, demonstrations were collected using expert policies trained via reinforcement learning (RL).

### Latency-Aware Evaluation Protocol
The centerpiece is the delay blocking mechanism. Using the Real-Time Factor (RTF), which is the ratio of simulation time to real time, millisecond-level inference latency measured on real hardware is accurately converted into simulation delay steps and injected into the environment. The evaluation supports both "synchronous" inference (where the robot waits until inference finishes) and "asynchronous" inference (where the robot continues executing the previous action chunk while the next inference runs in the background), allowing systematic analysis under configurable latency.

captions.F2: Diagram illustrating execution timelines for synchronous and asynchronous inference, and how ReflexBench reproduces inference latency in simulation. Simulating the robot waiting or continuing previous actions during latency duration ($K$) faithfully mimics the impact of real-world delays.

sections.heading: A Fast, Forward-Looking 1B Model: Three Pillars Behind ReflexVLA
sections.summary: Based on a lightweight 1B foundation model, this section explains the architecture of ReflexVLA, which integrates latent future prediction, intermediate temporal fusion in the vision backbone, and inference optimizations like CUDA Graph.
sections.details:
ReflexVLA adopts a compact VLA-Adapter structure based on a combined DINOv2 and SigLIP vision backbone ($224\times 224$ resolution) and a 0.5B language model, Qwen2.5-0.5B. While maintaining a lightweight size of around 1B parameters overall, it incorporates three key designs.

### 1. Latent Future Prediction
In dynamic tasks, reacting purely to the current image is not enough; predicting the near future state is critical. However, reconstructing future RGB images at the pixel level requires huge compute and causes the model to focus on task-irrelevant background details. Instead, ReflexVLA pre-extracts future latent representations using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. The model takes in $H$ learnable future tokens (matching the action chunk horizon), projects the transformer output features into the DINOv3 feature space, and trains with a cosine similarity loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{future}}$). Adding only a single prediction token per step yields future-aware representations with virtually zero computational overhead.

### 2. Multi-Frame Temporal Fusion in Vision Features
Understanding object motion (velocity and direction) requires observing multiple past frames. However, tokenizing all past images and feeding them to the language model causes the self-attention compute to explode quadratically with token count. ReflexVLA therefore fuses temporal features inside intermediate layers of the vision backbone before passing them to the language model. Intermediate layers are chosen because they preserve rich local textures and motion cues better than deeper, highly semantic layers. Features across past $T$ frames at matching patch locations are aggregated with causal attention and added to the current frame features. This keeps the visual token count passed to the language model identical to a single frame while supplying rich motion information.

### 3. Inference Latency Optimization
No matter how good a decision is, late output causes the robot to collide. The authors introduced two thorough implementation-level speedups. First, batched visual encoding: instead of passing multiple camera views across past frames through the encoder separately, all images are batched together onto the GPU. Second, CUDA Graph replay: the entire static computation graph from image input through the language model to the action head is captured as a CUDA Graph, running inference simply by updating memory buffers and replaying the graph. Completely eliminating fine-grained CPU kernel launch overheads dramatically cuts inference latency without altering model architecture or weights.

captions.F3: Architecture overview of ReflexVLA. Multi-frame image features are temporally fused in intermediate ViT layers (top left) and trained with an auxiliary latent future prediction task using frozen DINOv3 (middle). At inference, batched processing and CUDA Graph replay (right) deliver fast responses.

sections.heading: Empirical Results: Outreacting 7B Models and Validating on Real Hardware
sections.summary: Evaluated across ReflexBench, the static LIBERO benchmark, and a real robot arm. Despite its compact 1B size, ReflexVLA halved inference latency and outperformed 7B-scale models and existing dynamic VLAs with high success rates.
sections.details:
Experiments compare ReflexVLA against lightweight models (SmolVLA, VLA-Adapter), dynamic methods (DynamicVLA, PUMA), and large models (OpenVLA-OFT 7B, $\pi_{0.5}$ 4B). All models were trained under the same setting on 200 demonstration episodes per task and evaluated on a single NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada GPU.

### Optimal Control Parameters (Q1)
Using the lightweight SmolVLA, the authors first analyzed inference frequencies and control settings. At higher inference frequencies, asynchronous inference (computing the next step while executing the previous output) outperformed synchronous inference. Furthermore, predicting a larger action chunk size of 8 while keeping the execution horizon short at 2 steps before re-inferring proved most effective for tracking fast environmental changes.

### Performance on ReflexBench (Q2)
Across the six ReflexBench tasks, ReflexVLA achieved an average success rate of 50.4%, ranking top among all compared models. This is an improvement of over 20 percentage points from its base VLA-Adapter (30.3%). Notably, it substantially outpaced the 7B OpenVLA-OFT (22.2%) and 4B $\pi_{0.5}$ (34.8%), and surpassed PUMA (48.7%), a 4B dynamic-specialized VLA. Even with less than a quarter of the parameters, fast inference and accurate future prediction allow it to surpass larger models.

### Generalization to Static Tasks (Q3)
To check whether specializing in dynamic tasks compromised static capabilities, the authors evaluated on the LIBERO benchmark. ReflexVLA reached an average success rate of 97.2%, maintaining performance on par with the base model (VLA-Adapter). Incorporating dynamic prediction mechanisms does not degrade general manipulation performance.

### Findings from Ablation Studies (Q4)
Ablating individual components yielded insightful findings:
- Future prediction target: Predicting end-to-end learnable features caused representation collapse and lower success, but targeting frozen DINOv3 features boosted the success rate sharply from 36.8% to 62.8%.
- Temporal fusion stage: Fusing features at intermediate layers outperformed late-stage fusion (71.7%), supporting the importance of local motion cues.
- Inference optimization: Applying batched encoding and CUDA Graph cut inference latency from 125.1 ms to 65.0 ms (nearly half), lifting the success rate further from 71.7% to 73.8%.

### Real-World Robot Experiments (Q5)
Using an AgileX Piper robot arm, ReflexVLA was tested on three physical tasks: Conveyor Belt Pick-and-Place, Whack-a-Mole, and Ball Catching. ReflexVLA decisively outperformed SmolVLA across all tasks, matching or exceeding PUMA, which is four times its size.

captions.F5: Grid search results over action chunk size and action horizon using SmolVLA. Under asynchronous inference (Async), pairing a larger chunk size (8 or 16) with a short execution horizon around 2 visually demonstrates superior success rates.
captions.F6: Real-world robot experiments on an AgileX Piper arm. From top to bottom: picking a cube from a conveyor belt, pressing illuminated buttons, and catching a rolling ball, executing dynamic tasks without delay.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Summarizes the value of latency-aware dynamic benchmark ReflexBench and the predictive, fast 1B model ReflexVLA, highlighting avenues for future work.
sections.details:
This paper introduced ReflexBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark that faithfully replicates real-world inference latency, establishing a new evaluation standard that decouples simulation stepping from control. In addition, the authors developed ReflexVLA, combining latent future prediction, intermediate temporal fusion, and system optimizations. With just 1B parameters, it delivers agile control that outperforms existing large VLAs across both simulation and real-world experiments.

The authors note two main future directions. First, future prediction and temporal fusion modules are currently introduced only during fine-tuning; incorporating them into large-scale robot pretraining could bring further gains. Second, while this work explored standard synchronous and asynchronous inference, integrating with more advanced real-time control frameworks such as RTC (Real-Time Chunking) could unlock even stronger latency tolerance.

takeaways: When evaluating dynamic environments in simulation, moving away from pausing the simulator clock and explicitly injecting real-world inference latency is essential.
Predicting the future in the latent feature space of a frozen foundation model (such as DINOv3) rather than raw pixels stably yields control-relevant representations without extra compute.
When processing multi-frame history, applying causal attention within intermediate layers of the vision backbone captures motion cues efficiently without bloating language model token counts.

Rather than scaling up model parameters, cutting inference latency down by milliseconds with CUDA Graphs and running high-frequency asynchronous updates has a far greater direct impact on dynamic task success.
limitations: The future prediction and intermediate temporal fusion modules are only trained during downstream task fine-tuning and were not part of large-scale robot dataset pretraining.
Only standard synchronous and asynchronous inference paradigms were evaluated, leaving integration with more advanced real-time execution schemes (such as RTC) unverified.
